summary.text: 少 is used for “few” or “less.” Early forms transcribed as 少 or 小 are reported for both “few” and “small”; a proposed picture of grains is not securely identified, and the evidence does not establish which meaning came first.

formation.text: The formation is disputed. One analysis treats the early graph as a picture of fine grains, perhaps sand, associated with “small” or “few”; the referent is unresolved. The received Shuowen account instead parses 少 as 小, meaning “small,” plus 丿 as a phonetic element. This is a historical analysis, not settled proof of the original design.

components.text: In the received Shuowen parsing, 小 contributes the idea “small.” Early 少 and 小 overlap in shape and use, so this account does not prove that 小 was a separate component in the original graph.
The received Shuowen parsing assigns 丿 a phonetic role in 少, but does not establish that the stroke belonged to the graph’s original design.

sound_limitation.text: The attested modern Mandarin pair does not establish the ancient sound relation proposed by the received Shuowen analysis.

sound.text: In modern Mandarin, 丿 is piě and 少 is shǎo. This current comparison does not confirm their proposed historical relation.

history.text: Early forms conventionally transcribed as 少 or 小 overlap in shape and use. Specialist accounts describe bronze forms with an added slanting stroke distinguishing 少 from 小, but the point when their uses became consistently distinct is uncertain. The curated oracle-style image is a modern redraw, not an artifact photograph, and does not establish what the strokes depict.

The received Shuowen explanation glosses 少 as “not many” and parses it as 小 plus phonetic 丿. Historical sound-series analyses disagree about whether 少 and 小 were related in pronunciation; reconstructions of 少 alone do not settle that question.

uncertainties.text: The early strokes’ referent—sand grains, rice grains, or something else—and whether “small” or “few” was the graph’s original meaning remain unresolved. The grain picture is a proposal.
The evidence does not establish a dated path connecting “small,” “few,” “young,” “insufficient,” and “short time.”

senses.period: Oracle-bone usage reported; bronze usage also reported, with precise dates unresolved
senses.text: Early forms transcribed as 少 or 小 are reported for “few”; bronze examples include use in contrast with 多. The evidence does not establish this as the earliest sense or its priority relative to “small.”

senses.period: Oracle-bone usage reported; bronze examples occur sometimes, with precise dates unresolved
senses.text: Early forms transcribed as 少 or 小 are also reported for “small,” and some bronze uses are reported. Their overlap does not establish which meaning came first.

senses.period: Bronze inscription usage reported; precise date unresolved
senses.text: Bronze examples and historical dictionary entries record “young” or “youthful”; how this sense developed is not established.
Historical dictionary entries record “short time”; its emergence and relation to the other meanings are unresolved.
Historical dictionary entries record “insufficient” or “lacking”; development from another sense is not established.

limitations.text: No precise earliest dated attestation or complete dated sequence of meanings is established. Early uses for “small” and “few” do not prove a developmental link; dictionary ordering is not chronology.

overview.text: 少 commonly means “few” or “less.” One proposal reads its early strokes as grains, perhaps sand, shown in small quantity; the referent is uncertain.

components.text: The received Shuowen parsing gives 小 the idea “small”; early overlap means it need not have been a separate original part.
The received Shuowen parsing assigns 丿 a sound role, though its place in the original graph is uncertain.

relationships.text: The received Shuowen analysis assigns 小 a semantic role in 少, while competing accounts treat early 少 and 小 as overlapping forms that may not have had this separate component structure.
The received Shuowen analysis assigns 丿 a phonetic role in 少. The modern Mandarin pair piě–shǎo does not establish that historical relation or confirm the original design.
